aspect: The argument that there is no such duty
description: Buxton and Gibney (Political Studies, 2025) argue no duty of gratitude is owed to the asylum state, because the state-imposed barriers and hardships refugees must endure to reach asylum undermine it. Any gratitude is owed instead to those who helped them evade those restrictions - and resentment is often the more apt response.
energy_note: Permission, from a journal, to stop performing.
source_name: Must Refugees Be Grateful?, Political Studies

aspect: Gratitude as a debt that never clears
description: Mimi Nguyen's framing treats gratitude as a social emotion binding refugees to the state in an 'endless cycle of debt repayment'. Refuge is framed as a conditional gift demanding repayment.
energy_note: A gift you are still paying for twenty years later.

aspect: EXAMPLE - told publicly that you owe
description: Tucker Carlson claimed in 2020 that Rep. Ilhan Omar, resettled in 1995, still owed duties of gratitude to the US that should shape how she behaves and feels - twenty-five years later, as a sitting member of Congress.
energy_note: Elected, and still asked to say thank you.

description: Dina Nayeri's The Ungrateful Refugee recounts people who assumed she was grateful, or thought she ought to be. The book exists because the expectation is universal enough to name.
source_name: The Ungrateful Refugee, via Buxton & Gibney

aspect: The double bind for the competent
description: A skilled migrant who arrived by every rule, paid every fee and was refused repeatedly is still expected to speak of the destination as a rescue. Describing it accurately - as a transaction he mostly funded - reads as arrogance.

Someone says 'you must be so happy to be here' and Omid says yes. He is thinking about the twenty-six months, the CAD 7,500, the father he did not bury. He says yes because the alternative is a conversation he will lose.
energy_note: Agreeing, because disagreeing costs more than it is worth.

aspect: It also lands on the host
description: Research on Ukrainian refugees in Poland - 30 refugees and 24 hosts - found hosts experienced gratitude variably, including as a burden producing awkwardness. The expectation damages both sides of the exchange.
notes: Useful nuance: this is not simply hosts being cruel.
